query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An on‐the‐fly active learning thermodynamic integration method that continuously refines a machine‐learned interatomic potential using sparse ab initio data and physical constraints (including vibrational and electron–vibration coupling) will yield accurate free energy surfaces for both solid and liquid phases near fusion conditions at a computational cost an order of magnitude lower than full ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (e.g., Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni-based systems with up to five to six principal components) in their equilibrium solid and liquid states near the melting temperature.
generation.intervention: Implement an active learning workflow that on-the-fly trains and updates a machine-learned interatomic potential using sparse ab initio data while incorporating enhanced sampling techniques that explicitly capture vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling during thermodynamic integration.
generation.conditions: The method is applied over a temperature range approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the nominal melting temperature and for alloy compositions with up to five or six principal elements.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolving machine-learned potential that is periodically recalibrated in the transition region serves as the mediator, ensuring that phase boundaries and coupling effects are faithfully captured.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling explores both solid and liquid phase configurations while active learning dynamically updates the potential using sparse, targeted ab initio data. This delivers accurate free energy differences while drastically reducing the number of costly ab initio MD steps required to sample vibrational and electron–vibration effects compared to traditional methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: The proposed method will predict the fusion free energies and derived properties (such as enthalpy and entropy of fusion) with an accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio MD (within about 5% error) but with a computational expense roughly ten times lower than that of current TOR-TILD or direct MD approaches.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations and TOR-TILD methods, which fully capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration effects but are extremely computationally intensive, especially for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid for high-entropy alloy systems near melting (0.8–1.2 Tm) with up to six principal components. Its performance in systems with extreme compositions or where electronic correlations dominate remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the method’s ability to precisely capture the electron–vibration coupling in highly anharmonic regimes and potential instabilities in the active learning retraining process under rapid phase transitions.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative high-entropy alloy (e.g., an Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system) and perform free energy evaluations using both the on‐the‐fly active learning thermodynamic integration method and a baseline explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD workflow over the temperature range 0.8 to 1.2 Tm. Compare the predicted free energy surfaces, fusion enthalpy, and entropy values between the two methods.
measurements: Free energy differences between solid and liquid phases
Fusion enthalpy and entropy of fusion obtained from thermodynamic integration
Computational time and number of required ab initio MD steps
Vibrational density of states and related electron–vibration coupling indicators
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the active learning method yields free energy differences or fusion properties that deviate by more than approximately 5% from the baseline method or does not achieve a computational speed-up of roughly tenfold, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.2. Thermodynamic Descriptions of Ta-Cr and Ta-V Binary Systems
cited_evidence.text: Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by several research groups [,,,,]. In these thermodynamic modeling, the Gibbs energy of pure elements were taken from SGTE (Scientific Group Thermodata Europe) data [], which is also known as the second generation of thermodynamic description. In this description, the Gibbs energy was expressed as empirical temperature polynomials and valid only down to 298 K. In this section, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically re-assessed by utilizing the above established third-generation Gibbs energy expressions for pure Cr and V as well as those for Ta from our previous work []. In addition, an effective strategy to obtain Gibbs energy for Laves phase was proposed and applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V systems. Since the experimental phase equilibrium and thermodynamic properties in the Ta-Cr binary system have been recently reviewed by Jiang et al. [], their reviewed data were adopted in the present modeling. As for the Ta-V binary system, most of the reported data have been reviewed by Danon and Servant [] (2004). Thus, only the latest experimental data in the Ta-V binary system available in

The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.

decision.trend: Starting around 2018 (PMC6207727), first-principles and Monte Carlo methods were combined to capture phase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys. Subsequent work (PMC9119285) incorporated both vibrational and configurational entropy to assess thermodynamic stability, though the liquid phase and complete electron–vibration coupling remained underexplored. A high-fidelity, high-throughput approach for screening large composition spaces followed (PMC9279411), but did not fully solve the challenge of evaluating liquid-phase free energies. Later studies (PMC11336915) focused on thermodynamic modeling of rapid solidification processes but still relied on empirical formulas or partial thermochemical models. Most recently (PMC11275555), an ab initio-based, multi-objective optimization framework emerged, integrating electronic structure and machine-learned interatomic potentials. Despite these advances, capturing fully coupled vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration effects in both solid and liquid phases at near-fusion conditions remains prohibitively expensive and is still an open challenge for high-entropy materials.
decision.unsolved: A seamless, yet computationally feasible methodology that retains all major energetic and entropic contributions in both solid and liquid near-fusion states of high-entropy alloys is lacking. Existing methods either suffer from cost and scalability issues (explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD) or omit critical anharmonic and electron–vibration coupling contributions.
decision.lever: Deploy an on-the-fly active learning thermodynamic-integration method that trains a machine-learned interatomic potential on sparse ab initio data while explicitly encoding vibrational and electron–vibration coupling. The workflow performs enhanced sampling for both solid and liquid states, automatically refining potential fidelity in the transition region, and then uses thermodynamic integration to obtain full free-energy surfaces.
decision.why: By combining ab initio reference data and physics-based constraints with a machine-learned interatomic potential, this approach can capture vibrational and electronic couplings at a fraction of the cost of full ab initio molecular-dynamics or TOR-TILD. The composition and temperature range can encompass up to five to six principal components (e.g., Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–X) over 0.8 to 1.2 of the nominal melting temperature. Decisive validation would measure the free energy difference between the solid and liquid phases (plus derived properties like the enthalpy of fusion and entropy contributions) and compare these predictions to those from baseline ab initio MD or TOR-TILD to confirm accuracy and expose any discrepancies.
